Name: attributed_belief_geometry
Title: Whose Belief Is It? Probing and Steering the Internal Geometry of Attributed Beliefs in LLMs
Short Hypothesis: LLMs maintain internal representations not just of whether a statement is true (a 'truth direction'), but of *who* holds a given belief, and these agent-attributed belief states are encoded along partially separable, causally-manipulable directions distinct from the model's own factual-veracity direction. We hypothesize that failures in tracking false beliefs of others (Theory-of-Mind errors) arise from collapse or entanglement of these attributed-belief directions with the model's own knowledge direction.
Related Work: Prior probing work (Savcisens & Eliassi-Rad 2025 'Trilemma of Truth'; Schouten et al. 2024 'truth directions are context sensitive'; Marks & Tegmark) identifies veracity/truth directions in activation space. Ferrando et al. 2024 finds entity 'do-I-know-this' directions. Wang et al. 2025 mechanistically explains sycophancy as override of learned knowledge. The referenced paper (Language models cannot reliably distinguish belief from knowledge and fact) shows behavioral confusion between belief and fact. All of these treat belief/truth as a single (or self-centered) axis. NONE isolate the *agent-attribution* dimension: whether the model separately encodes 'I believe X', 'Alice believes X', 'Bob believes not-X' as distinct, addressable representations, nor whether false-belief Theory-of-Mind failures are mechanistically explained by entanglement between an attributed-belief direction and the model's own factual direction. We reframe belief-tracking as a multi-agent geometric problem and provide causal steering interventions, which is a genuinely new lens.
Abstract: Language models are increasingly used as agents that must reason about what different parties believe, yet recent work shows they cannot reliably distinguish belief from knowledge and fact. We investigate a finer question: does an LLM internally represent *whose* belief a proposition is, and are these attributed beliefs encoded separately from the model's own factual knowledge? Using controlled false-belief scenarios (Sally-Anne style and factual-disagreement dialogues) across several open-weight models, we train linear probes to recover (a) the truth-value the model assigns a proposition and (b) the belief a specified agent holds about it. We find that agent-attributed belief is recoverable along directions partially orthogonal to the model's own veracity direction, and that Theory-of-Mind failures coincide with high alignment (entanglement) between these directions in deeper layers. We then perform causal activation-patching and steering: adding the attributed-belief direction for agent A causally shifts the model's answers to 'what does A think?' without changing its answer to 'what is true?', while forcing entanglement induces egocentric errors. We propose an 'attribution-disentanglement' regularizer during light fine-tuning that increases the separation of self- vs. other-belief subspaces and measurably improves false-belief accuracy without harming factual QA. Our results recast belief-tracking failures as a geometric entanglement problem and offer a cheap, interpretable intervention. All experiments run on <=8B models feasible for an academic lab.
Experiments: 1) Dataset construction: Build controlled scenarios with (i) classic false-belief tasks (object moved while agent absent), (ii) multi-agent factual-disagreement dialogues where two named agents assert contradictory claims and one contradicts a known fact, (iii) matched 'ground-truth' probes. Each item yields three query types: 'Is X true?', 'What does agent A believe about X?', 'What does agent B believe about X?'. ~2-3k items, templated with entity swaps. 2) Probing: On models (Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, plus a base vs chat pair), extract residual-stream activations at the token positions of each query. Train linear/logistic probes for (a) model's own truth judgment, (b) each agent's attributed belief. Measure probe accuracy per layer, and compute cosine similarity / subspace overlap (principal angles) between the self-truth direction and each attributed-belief direction. 3) Entanglement-vs-error analysis: Correlate per-example ToM answer correctness with the layerwise alignment between attributed-belief and self-truth directions; test whether high alignment predicts egocentric (reality-biased) errors. 4) Causal interventions: (a) Activation patching — patch the attributed-belief subspace from a correct-belief example into an error case; measure whether the 'what does A think?' answer flips while the factual answer stays fixed. (b) Steering — add/subtract the recovered attributed-belief direction and measure controllability (answer flip rate) and specificity (leakage into factual answers). 5) Disentanglement fine-tuning: Add a lightweight LoRA fine-tune with a regularizer penalizing overlap between self and other belief subspaces (or an auxiliary contrastive loss on the belief-attribution probe); evaluate false-belief accuracy, factual QA (retain set: MMLU subset, TriviaQA), and probe separation before/after. Metrics: probe accuracy, principal-angle separation, ToM accuracy, steering flip-rate and specificity, retained factual accuracy.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Linear probes may not fully capture belief attribution if it is nonlinear or distributed; mitigated by also trying MLP probes and reporting negative results as informative. 2) Templated data may induce shortcut features (agent names/positions) rather than genuine belief representations; mitigated by entity/position randomization and control probes. 3) The self- vs other-belief directions may not be cleanly separable in small models, which itself would be a publishable finding. 4) Causal patching could have off-target effects; specificity metrics quantify this. 5) Disentanglement fine-tuning might trade off factual accuracy; we explicitly measure retention. 6) Results may vary across model families, requiring careful reporting rather than universal claims.
